title: Sodium 109 at 2 a.m.
note: Fictional patient. Values and doses follow the module’s cited guideline and are illustrative; local protocol and the attending’s judgment come first.
intro: You are the attending nephrologist on call. At 02:10 on Saturday, the internal medicine resident, Dr. Mendoza, calls from the ward. Mr. Felix Garcia, 54, drinks heavily, has eaten little for two weeks, and has been vomiting for three days. His sodium is 109 mmol/L and potassium 2.9 mmol/L. He had a generalized seizure 20 minutes ago and is now drowsy but breathing well.

n1.prompt: What do you tell Dr. Mendoza to give now?

choices.text: 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes, repeated up to twice, aiming for a rise of about 5 mmol/L; monitored bed.
choices.feedback: Seizure and reduced consciousness make this severely symptomatic hyponatremia. A small, fast rise of about 5 mmol/L relieves brain swelling; the 2014 European guideline sets this bolus approach.
choices.then: After two boluses, at 03:00, his sodium is 114 mmol/L and he is more alert.

choices.text: One liter of 0.9% saline over an hour, which raises sodium more gently and avoids the risk of overcorrecting, then recheck.
choices.feedback: Isotonic saline raises sodium slowly and unpredictably, too slowly for a patient who has just seized. Severe symptoms call for hypertonic boluses.
choices.then: You change the order to 3% saline boluses. After two, at 03:00, his sodium is 114 mmol/L and he is more alert.

choices.text: Fluid restriction, and recheck the sodium in the morning.
choices.feedback: A seizure is a severe symptom. Waiting risks further seizures, brain swelling, and respiratory arrest. Fluid restriction alone is far too slow.
choices.then: Dr. Mendoza calls back ten minutes later: another brief seizure. You order 3% saline boluses. After two, at 03:00, sodium is 114 mmol/L.

n2.prompt: He has improved. What do you write in the order now?

choices.text: Stop the boluses; write a 24-hour ceiling well inside 10 mmol/L, two-hourly sodium, hourly urine, and call-back triggers.
choices.feedback: Alcohol use, malnutrition, and low potassium raise the risk of osmotic demyelination. Potassium replacement also raises the sodium. The ward team will hold him overnight, so the numbers must be in writing.

choices.text: No ceiling is needed: a 2025 meta-analysis found faster correction was associated with fewer deaths, so let the sodium rise as it will.
choices.feedback: That analysis was observational, and sicker patients may have been corrected more slowly. It argues against needless caution, not against the ceiling. Osmotic demyelination is irreversible.
choices.then: You write the ceiling and the check times after all.

choices.text: Tell Dr. Mendoza by phone to “go slowly from here” and check sodium in the morning.
choices.feedback: “Slowly” is not a number, and a morning check is too late to catch overcorrection. Leave the ceiling, the check times, and the call-back triggers in the written order.
choices.then: You call back and dictate the ceiling, two-hourly sodium checks, and the call-back triggers.

n3.scene: At 06:00 Dr. Mendoza calls back: sodium 121 mmol/L, and he has passed 1.8 liters of dilute urine since 03:00. He is alert and asking for breakfast.

choices.text: Stop all saline, give desmopressin with 5% dextrose, check sodium every 2 hours, and come in.
choices.feedback: A rise of 12 mmol/L in four hours has already crossed the 24-hour limit. As the cause resolves, a water diuresis can overcorrect faster than any infusion. The rescue brings the sodium back down.

choices.text: Stop the saline, encourage oral fluids, and recheck the sodium at noon when the day team is in.
choices.feedback: Stopping the saline is not enough: the dilute urine keeps raising the sodium. He is already over the limit, and a six-hour gap allows more.
choices.then: You call back, order desmopressin with 5% dextrose, and two-hourly sodium checks.

choices.text: Good progress. Continue; he looks well.
choices.feedback: Looking well now says nothing about osmotic demyelination, which appears days later and is irreversible. The rise has already crossed the limit, and the water diuresis is pushing it further.
choices.then: The nurse questions the plan. You order desmopressin with 5% dextrose and two-hourly checks.

n4.scene: You will see him at 09:00. The ward team carries the plan until then.
n4.prompt: What must the resident be able to repeat back?

choices.text: What to give, how often to check sodium and urine, and the numbers that trigger a call.
choices.feedback: Before you hang up, the caller should be able to repeat three things: what to give now, how the problem leaves (or enters) the body, and the number that makes them call you back.

choices.text: “Call me if anything changes, if he gets worse, or if you are worried about him at any point before I come in.”
choices.feedback: “Anything” leaves the threshold to a tired resident at 6 a.m. Give the numbers.

choices.text: Nothing; it is in the order sheet.
choices.feedback: A read-back confirms the plan was understood, not just written. It takes thirty seconds.

n5.scene: On Sunday at 02:00, 24 hours after the start, his sodium is 117 mmol/L, a rise of 8. The team asks for the plan for the second day.

choices.text: A ceiling of 8 mmol/L for the next 24 hours, continued checks, and a watch for new neurologic signs.
choices.feedback: The guideline limit is 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 in each 24 hours after. Osmotic demyelination, if it occurs, appears days later, so the team needs to know what to look for.

choices.text: He is out of danger; correct freely to normal today.
choices.feedback: The limit applies each day until the sodium is safe. His risk factors have not changed.

choices.text: Same plan as yesterday: the same 24-hour ceiling, the same two-hourly checks, and the same call-back triggers.
choices.feedback: Close, but the second-day limit is lower: 8 mmol/L in each 24 hours after the first. Write it.

end.title: Day 4
end.text: By day 4 his sodium is 131 mmol/L. He eats, walks, and talks normally. You document the timeline, the overcorrection and its rescue, and the cause: poor intake, alcohol, and vomiting. Alcohol counseling and nutrition support are arranged before discharge.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Severe symptoms get hypertonic boluses aiming for a rise of about 5 mmol/L.
  • Write the ceiling in the order: 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours, 8 in each 24 hours after, well inside it when risk is high.
  • Watch the urine. A water diuresis can overcorrect faster than any infusion; have desmopressin with 5% dextrose ready.
  • Leave the numbers in writing and have the caller repeat them back.

See Physiology, Evidence and What the attending does.
